stimuli.text: A block of mass 3 kg on a 20° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 3 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.2. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 1.7 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.13\cos(9t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) and a solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.7 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 70$$ N/m is compressed 0.18 m and launches a 1 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
The ½ appears on both sides.
Take the square root.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 5x^3$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 0$$ m to $$x = 2$$ m?

options.why: Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate rather than differentiate.
The force is not constant.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 60 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 13 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Recheck the average.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
The average angular speed is ω₀/2.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 70 kg load 8 m at constant speed in 22 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: Correct. P = mgh/t.
Include g.
P = W/t.
That is the work; divide by time.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 85$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: The ratio is m/k.
Include the 2π.
That is the frequency.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -100x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: ω is the square root of the coefficient.
T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.
T = 2π/ω.
Correct. ω = √100 = 10 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.

questions.stem: Masses of 9 kg and 5 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: Use T = m₂(g + a).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 120 m wide, moving at 5 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 2 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.

questions.stem: A planet has 4 times Earth's mass and 0.5 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: g decreases with radius.
Correct. g ∝ M/R².
The ratio is inverted.
g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 12 m high at 11 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Take the square root for the time.
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Fall time is √(2h/g).

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 1t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 7 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its velocity at $$t = 5$$ s?

options.why: Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.
Include the initial velocity.
Correct. Integrate a(t) and add the initial velocity.
The acceleration is not constant, so constant-acceleration equations do not apply.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1.8 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
I = mL²/3.
A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = 4t^3 - 2t^2 + 2t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 4$$ s?

options.why: Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.
Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.

questions.explanation: a(t) = 24t - 4, so at t = 4 the value is 92.

questions.stem: A uniform 7 m beam weighing 400 N rests on supports at both ends. A 200 N load sits 5 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
The load is not at the center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.
Include the beam's weight at its center.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$4 \times 10^{24}$$ kg and radius $$5 \times 10^{6}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 6 rad/s and amplitude 0.15 m. What is its speed when it is 0.12 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
Use A² − x² under a square root.

questions.stem: A 0.8 kg ball hits a wall at 6 m/s and rebounds at 2 m/s. The contact lasts 0.09 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Divide by time.
Include the rebound.

questions.stem: A 6 kg cart moving at 7 m/s collides with and sticks to a 4 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: The carts share the momentum.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 6·7/10 = 4.2 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 58.8 J.

questions.stem: A 4 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 6 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
I/R² = M/2.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
For a disk, I/R² = M/2.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 5.6 m/s².

questions.stem: A block slides down a 30° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.1. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction acts up the slope.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).

questions.stem: A constant torque of 19 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 0.8$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 6 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: Convert revolutions to radians.
W = ½Iω².
Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
½Iω² = W; solve for ω.

questions.stem: A 6 kg ball moving at +10 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 1 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 1 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: That would be a sticking collision.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
Only equal masses exchange velocities.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = 7.14 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 17.1 m/s.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 3$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^2$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: The rod is not uniform.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 21 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its time of flight?

options.why: Use v₀ sin θ.
Use the vertical component.
Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
That is the time to the top; the flight is twice as long.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 18.2 m/s, v₀y = 10.5 m/s. T = 2v₀y/g = 2.14 s.

questions.stem: What is the rotational inertia of a uniform rod of mass 1 kg and length 1 m about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod?

options.why: That is a disk's formula.
Correct. I = ML²/3 (parallel-axis theorem from ML²/12).
The mass is spread along the rod.
That is about the center.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 50 N/m and 80 N/m are connected in series and support a 1.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: The force is the weight, mg.
Both springs share the load.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.
Correct. k_eq = k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).

questions.stem: A 55 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating upward at 1 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Check the direction of the acceleration.
Include gravity.

questions.stem: A 5 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 8t^2$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 4$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Divide by the mass to get speed.
Integrate the force over time.
The force is not constant.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 9 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital speed to A's?

options.why: Farther satellites move more slowly.
Correct. v = √(GM/r), so v ∝ r^(−1/2).

questions.stem: A 2500 kg car heading east at 10 m/s collides with a 500 kg car heading north at 10 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Weight each velocity by its mass.
Divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 3.8 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².
Some energy goes into rotation.
That is only correct for a hoop.

questions.stem: A 1.5 kg ball on a 1.5 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 6 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Centripetal force uses v².
Include gravity.
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 4x^3 - 27x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Take the square root.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 12x² − 27 = 0 gives x = 1.5 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 2.4 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
The weight acts at L/2.
τ = MgL/2.
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 10 m down a 20° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Friction removes energy.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.1 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.05$$ kg/s. What is the time constant of its approach to terminal speed?

options.why: Correct. From m dv/dt = mg − bv, τ = m/b.
τ = m/b.
That is the terminal speed.
τ has units of seconds: m/b.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 19.6 m/s and τ = m/b = 2 s.

questions.stem: A 6 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 1 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.1. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Friction opposes the motion.
Include friction on the table block.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 4 kg and radius 0.4 m spins at 15 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: The clay's inertia is mR².
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
Use rotational inertias, not masses.
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 3x^3 - 36x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Take the square root.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 9x² − 36 = 0 gives x = 2 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A 21 g bullet moving at 390 m/s embeds in a 1.1 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: h = V²/(2g).
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Find the block's speed after the collision first.

questions.explanation: V = 7.31 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 2.72 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 3 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 0.5 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.13 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.

rubric.example: solid cylinder: 4.71 m/s; solid sphere: 4.88 m/s

parts.prompt: Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
